en: Preface to the *Xutang Lu*:
Before the empty kalpa, there was a handless man who entered the shadowless forest and gathered from the rootless tree.

Facing the monastery of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), he relied upon the treasury of radiance (*ābhāsvara-kośa*) to lay the foundation pillars of precept, concentration, and wisdom, and to erect the ridgepoles and beams of essence, attributes, and function.
Liberation is its gate; the operation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) is its seat. It is called the "Empty Hall," where my teacher, Linquan, resides.
At the end of the Zen heavens, I beheld Danxia playing with shadows; yet even as he clarifies the mind through form, one cannot avoid pointing at emptiness and speaking of emptiness.
Whether speaking horizontally or vertically, I seek to reach the place of intimacy, so that those who hear may daily and seasonally practice until they become vast and enlightened.
This is the work of the Spiritually Enlightened.

The First Case:
The Stages of Qingyuan (Study and Practice), read by the late student Xingyi. Carved by Shengsheng Daoren.

He addressed the assembly, saying: "Where there is cultivation and progress, one may debate high and low; where there is neither realization nor conditioned action, how could there be rising or falling?
As for those who do not step outside their door when walking, nor occupy the hall when sitting—where, then, would you arrange them?"
[The text] cites Zen Master Qingyuan Si’s question to the Great Master Huineng: "What should one apply oneself to so as not to fall into stages?
(If this side is secure, that side will naturally correspond. The Master said: "What have you been doing? (Thoroughly fathoming the subtle principle and minutely discerning the source.)

Sengtsai said, "I do not even take the Noble Truths" (as if there were still this [something] remaining). The Patriarch asked, "In what rank or level do you fall? (Layer upon layer of refinement; one must recognize the refined gold.

Sengtsai said, "If I do not even take the Noble Truths, in what rank or level would I fall? (Without skin or fur, there is no standing; when the sentiments of sage and ordinary are exhausted. The Patriarch said:
It is so, it is so (the true does not conceal the false; the crooked does not hide the straight). Guard and maintain yourself well.
I shall now offer these verses (spoken in the vernacular out of compassion): The ground of the mind contains all seeds; When the rain falls everywhere, they all sprout.
Sudden awakening to the nature of the flower [is achieved simply by letting the snow melt]; the fruit of Bodhi is spontaneously realized [as spring naturally arrives].
The Master said: "Within the gate of transformative teaching, there is no lack of evaluation; yet upon the ground of ultimate reality, how could there be any gradations?

From beginning to end, returning to the root and restoring the source, those who attain the Dharma-body without passing through kalpas know for themselves that they have transcended both the sudden and the gradual."
Transcending the most profound and mysterious ultimate principles, the Sixth Patriarch one day said to the assembly:
"Virtuous friends, each of you should purify your minds and listen to my teaching of the Dharma. You all should know that your own minds are the Buddha; do not harbor further doubt."
Externally there is not a single thing that can be established; all are various phenomena produced by the fundamental mind.
Thus the Sūtra says: "When the mind arises, various phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, various phenomena cease.

If one wishes to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*), one must attain the samādhi of the single characteristic and the samādhi of the single practice. If, in all places, one does not dwell upon characteristics, then those characteristics—
Within this state, neither aversion nor affection arises, nor is there any grasping or rejecting. One does not dwell upon matters such as benefit or ruin, success or failure.
Serene, tranquil, empty, harmonious, and pure—this is called the Samādhi of the Single Characteristic.

If, in all places—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—one maintains a purely straightforward mind, the site of practice becomes immovable and is truly realized as a Pure Land; this is called the Samādhi of the Single Practice. If a person possesses...
The second is samādhi. Just as the earth possesses seeds that can contain, nurture, and bring them to fruition, so too are the single characteristic and the single practice.
My preaching of the Dharma now is like seasonal rain that thoroughly moistens the great earth. Your Buddha-nature is like these various seeds;
encountering this soaking moisture, they shall all sprout and grow. Those who receive my intent will certainly attain Bodhi.
"Those who rely on my practice will surely realize the wondrous fruit. Linsuan said: "Do not blame Old Lu for being able to administer medicine;
having long been accustomed to seeing it take effect, I dare to transmit the prescription. Bodhidharma also said: "I have come to this land to preach the Dharma and save deluded minds. Linsuan said:
"The ancients and those of later generations possessed a most earnest, grandmotherly heart; how much more so Danxia, whose [teaching] was continuous and dense?"
The verse that clarifies the difficulty of distinguishing the hidden is presented as follows:

"Standing alone, it is difficult to peer at with the true eye; (only those who cast a sidelong glance have a share). Transcending past and present, what kind could possibly match it? (Indeed, one sees them all out of step.
Moss covers the ancient hall, no one attends; (the jade palace is deep and silent. The moon locks Cangwu, the phoenix does not perch; (who would ever dare to settle there?)”
The Master said: "Within the shadows of multicolored clouds, an immortal appears; holding a red silk fan, he covers his face. You must quickly turn your eyes to look at the immortal;
do not look at the fan in the immortal's hand. There are some starving-eyed Chan practitioners who greedily gaze at the moon beyond the clouds, yet lose the pearl in their own palms.
They idly pursue every phrase and seek out words, failing to strive for knowing the root and reaching the source—how much more so in this case!
One who does not fall into any hierarchical rank is磊磊落落 (li lè luò luò), majestic and imposing. His mechanism cannot be touched;
his edge cannot be met. When employed, he acts; when set aside, he hides. He is lively and agile, revolving and turning.
Although he enters and exits through the gateway of the face, he leaves no form or shadow, making it difficult to examine him in detail. This is why it is so difficult to apply the True Eye to him.
Is it not something that cannot be peered into or encroached upon? Therefore, when Linji entrusted San-sheng, he said:
"After my passing, you must not extinguish my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye. San-sheng replied: "How would I dare extinguish the Master’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye?
Linji asked: "If someone were to ask you suddenly, how would you respond? San-sheng then gave a shout. Linji said: "Who would have known my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye?"
The Treasury of the Eye was extinguished before this blind donkey. Linquan said: "Who knows the place where the mouth is bitter but the heart is sweet?
He drives the wedge out and pulls the head back to leave him wide open. As for Sanxian’s shout like this—can the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye be glimpsed or not?
Is it seen through or not? Everyone, try looking up with a furrowed brow and see! In truth, from antiquity until now, this matter...
Now, analogies are difficult to find that can equal it; words and speech cannot reach it, like moss covering an ancient hall or the moon locking the azure peaks of Cangwu.

Your servant hesitates, unable to attend upon such majesty; the phoenix folds its wings and ascends secretly into the clouds and mists. Furthermore, as for the phrase "the Way does not fall within the realm of merit," how should one speak of it?
When the sentiments of sage and ordinary are exhausted, what need is there to establish rungs on a ladder?
Case Two: Shitou at Caoxi (Addressing the Assembly).

He said to the assembly: "The person has no heart to harm the tiger; the tiger has no intent to injure the person. When the halberds are turned back and the spears overturned, the strategy is secure and all-encompassing.
I do not know who possesses such a tactical plan."
Master Shitou Xiqian asked Qingyuan, "Since you left Caoxi, Master, when did you arrive here?
(The child is spoiled by the wealth of his father. Qingyuan said, "I do not know when you left Caoxi.

(By the power of Avalokiteśvara's mindfulness, the result returns to the person themselves. Shitou said, "I have not come from Caoxi. (To avoid the red, he speaks of the white. Qingyuan said, "I already know."

"You have reached the end of your journey" (it is difficult to deceive those with clear eyes). The Head said, "Venerable Sir, as you are a great man, please do not act so hastily" (tears and wailing may still be endured;
however, it is even more difficult to accept being buried in a mire of mud).
The Master said: "When Chan Master Xiqian of Shitou on Mount Nanyue first went to Jingju Temple on Mount Qingyuan in Jizhou to visit Master Si, Si asked, 'Where have you come from?
Xiqian replied, 'From Caoxi. Si asked, 'What have you brought with you?'"
Xuefeng said, "Even before reaching Caoxi, one does not lose it. Dongshan asked, "If that is so, what would you do with Caoxi?
Xuefeng replied, "If you had not gone there, how could you know you did not lose it? Xuefeng further asked, "Does the Great Master of Caoxi recognize you, O Master?
Dongshan asked, "Do you recognize me now? Xuefeng replied, "I recognize you, yet how could I truly recognize you? Dongshan said, "Though there be many horns, a single unicorn is sufficient."
Xian asked again, "Since you left Caoxi, Master, when did you arrive here? He replied, "I do not know when you left Caoxi.
Xian said, "I have never come from Caoxi. He said, "I already know where you came from.
Xian said, "Master, as you are a person of great stature, please do not speak so hastily. Linquan said, "Look closely!"
Lai’s gesture may seem like joining his palms while scolding his mother-in-law, yet it is unavoidable that he sees what is equal to the Master and thus reduces the Master’s virtue by half.

Only when one’s insight surpasses that of the Master is one fit for transmission; this is another way of expressing the principle that "a father conceals for his son, and a son conceals for his father," wherein the rectitude lies precisely therein.
This cannot be determined by worldly wisdom or cleverness. In reality, Lai has no place from which he comes, nor anywhere to which he goes.
There is no abiding. Thus the Sūtra says: "If anyone should say that the Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down, this person does not understand the meaning of what I have taught.
Why is this? The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore he is called the Tathāgata. Linquan said:
"As for Tathāgata Chan and Patriarchal Chan—enough with this quarreling over eyebrows and adzes!"
It is merely a single coin. Look further for the separate transmission of Danxia’s message. The verse says:
The wooden man comes to ask the way to the blue sky (pointing to emptiness while speaking of emptiness). The jade maiden is advanced in years and seems not to hear (the wind passing by her ear).

Hand in hand they walk together back to their native land (traveling together with no companions left behind). The evening mountains loom high, locked in heavy clouds (not allowing people to see; turning the wind).
[The text continues with] "The Master said: 'In the land of Chu, the seal of no-words was not transmitted; from Jetavana, a firm path sent a letter to arrive.

At such a time, for a wooden man to ask the way is to head toward the azure heavens in vain. Who would dare, at the crossroads, recklessly transmit news? Thus, the jade [remains] honored in its ancient state."
The woman hears the wind in the branches as if she does not hear; her teeth are missing as the clay ox plows through the moonlight as if she does not see.
Singing forth from within the void, she picks up whatever comes to hand. She shatters the mass of doubt and finishes her song of wild liberation.

Thus, she teaches one to depart from mind, intellect, and consciousness, and to investigate beyond the paths of the mundane and the sage. For those of shallow learning and shallow understanding, how can they avoid boring into her tongue?
Study! Those of narrow wisdom and narrow learning surely ought to glean from these words. These are all the very beginnings of the deluded thoughts that are the root of birth and death.
The ancients were exceedingly compassionate and their vows were vast and profound; they relied on words to reveal the wordless, and used non-explanation to make known true explanation.
They extended a single hand as a skillful means to provide guidance, intending to encourage those at the beginning of their practice with earnest diligence.

Toward it one proceeds; though the towering peaks of the evening mountain are difficult for the five eyes to discern, how can the brilliant radiance of the autumn moon fail to illuminate the inch-square mind?
To lock it away amidst heavy clouds is to needlessly constrain its agility; to linger at the profound barrier is to pointlessly allow procrastination.

If one releases a single thread to permit deliberation, I shall not begrudge the secret instruction that passes between my two brows. Do you understand this thoroughly? The wondrous essence is, from the beginning, non-existent.
As for the locus: throughout the entire body, how could there be any further trace?

"Walking, standing, sitting, and reclining are none other than wondrous function and spiritual power; speech and silence, manifest and subtle, are all the Dharma."
Regarding the Buddha-work of the gate: even if you were to take responsibility before the empty kalpa, you would still be cutting away the path to ask whether it exists or does not exist.
At this point, is it permitted to open your mouth?

"It has been a long time since you first 'marked the boat. I have returned to my quarters. When Xuefeng heard this, he attained realization. "A single thought turning back the light is identical to original attainment.

Hanging down his hand, he returns the device of the author; (this line-break signifies separation). Within ordinary speech, he unfurls the banners of his spear; (one must not meet him with the clash of arms).

Inquiring again, he proposes to return to the abbot’s quarters (*fāngzhàng*)—(once was pleasing, twice was shameful). With this single phrase made clear, there is no further doubt—(was it not nearly a missed opportunity once more?).
The Master said: "An old fisherman with embroidered robes goes to the market; his single leaf-like boat drifts upon the waves. Wansong said:
"This is one who enters the marketplace and extends a helping hand, not shying away from wind and waves.

Were it not for a master who knows the times, understands change, and possesses towering skillful means, one certainly could not discern the arrayed banners within ordinary speech. Were it not for relying on Mañjuśrī..."
He brandishes a sword, grasps a *bīmāra* staff, straps on the bow of Shigong, and looses the arrow of the National Teacher. He will surely suffer defeat and be forced to surrender.
Thus, he inquires once more, intending to press forward; he exerts all his strength to maintain his position and employs clever stratagems to seek a peaceful settlement.
Desiring to return to the Abbot’s quarters, he indeed attains clear and distinct realization at a single phrase. It may be said that one should think three times before thinking again. *Ei!*
Where the iron hammerhead with no hole is lightly raised, the mass of doubt is pulverized without remainder.
Case Sixteen: Jianyuan Holding a Shovel (at the time of his passing). He addressed the assembly, saying:

"To be cautious at the end and honor the distant past moves Heaven through filial piety; even to grind one's bones and crush one's body would be insufficient to repay such profound virtue. The monk...
The Master said, "The Sangha’s division of property need not be like this. If it were not for the ultimate principle, a single word would be perilous; do not labor your mind and strength in vain.
Has anyone here ever committed an error?
He then cited the case of Chan Master Jianyuan Xing, who one day took up a spade and went to Stone-Rain Hall, looking east and looking west.

[He] initiated a legal dispute. When Shuangjian saw this, he said, "What are you doing? [Pointing out the matter, he could not let it pass. Yuan said, "I am seeking the sacred relics of the former Master. [Does he still possess the eye of discernment?
Shuangjian said, "The vast waves are surging; white billows overflow the heavens. What 'sacred relics of the former Master' are you seeking?

[He knows only how to exhaust the law, yet disregards the lack of subjects. Yuan said, "This is precisely when one must exert effort. [When matters are difficult, only then does the heart of a true man manifest. Shuangjian said, "A single thing..."
There is no need for any effort of attachment (revealing everything without sparing one's lips). Yuan held a spade on his shoulder and walked away (a sharp monk turns at a single push).
Taoyuan Fu said, "The spiritual bones of the former master still remain" (it is difficult to deceive those with clear eyes).
The Master said: "Chan Master Jianyuan Zhongxing of Tanzhou served as an attendant to Daowu.
Once, while passing tea to Daowu, Daowu held up the cup and asked, 'Is this false or is it true? The Master crossed his hands and stepped forward, gazing intently at Daowu. Daowu said:"
"If it is wrong, it is entirely wrong; if it is right, it is entirely right. The Master said, "I do not speak in such a manner. [The monk] asked, "And how would you speak?
The Master snatched the cup away, held it up, and said, "Is this wrong or is this right? [The monk] said, "You are no longer merely my attendant. The Master then bowed. Linquan said:
"When chess meets a worthy opponent, there is no room for luck; when poetry reaches the point of being recited again, only then does its true meaning emerge."
Jian Gong was one day attending me when we went to a donor’s house for a funeral condolence. The Master struck the coffin and asked, "Is he alive?
Is he dead? I replied, "I will not say he is alive; I will not say he is dead. He asked, "Why do you not say? I said, "I will not say, I will not say.
On the way back, the Master said, "The Master must speak for me today. If you do not speak, I shall strike you."
"The Master has gone," [I] said. "Strike as you please; as for the Way, I shall not speak of it. The Master then struck me. Upon returning to the monastery, I said, "You should leave this place;
I fear that if the administrators find out, it will be inconvenient. The Master then paid his respects and took leave, retiring to Zhongyuan.
After three years had passed, he suddenly heard a youth reciting the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra, which reached the passage: "If one should attain [enlightenment] in the body of a bhikṣu..."
The Deliverer immediately manifested in the form of a bhikṣu. [Dongshan] suddenly attained great realization and, burning incense, prostrated from afar, saying:
"I now truly know that the late master’s final words were never in vain. It was only because I lacked understanding that I harbored resentment toward him. Now that the late master has passed away..."
"Only Shishuang is the legitimate successor; he will surely provide proof. Thereupon, the Master went to Shishuang. Upon seeing him, Shishuang asked, "Since leaving Daowu, where have you been?
The Master replied, "I have simply been staying at a village temple. Shishuang said, "Have you yet understood the karmic connection regarding the previous occasion when you struck the late master?
The Master rose and stepped forward, saying, "I beg the Master to speak a turning word for me. Shishuang said, "No."

[The Master] said, "I do not say he was born on the Path, nor do I say he died on the Path. The Master then recounted the circumstances of how [Linquan] had attained realization while staying at a village monastery.
Consequently, he paid his respects to Shishuang and prepared a vegetarian feast for him as an act of repentance. On another day, Linquan took up a spade and returned to Shishuang;
in the Dharma Hall, he walked from east to west and from west to east. Shishuang asked, "What are you doing? Linquan replied, "Not only did I examine..."
He asked about the origin of the matter, fearing he might again miss the point as before. [Linquan] said, "I am seeking the sacred relics of the former master.

Linquan said, "Judging from the past and looking at the present, this is very much like feigning compassion and pretending at filial piety. [The other] said, "The vast waves are immense and the white billows overflow the heavens;
what 'sacred relics of the former master' are you seeking? Linquan said, "One fights the difficult, not the easy. If one fights the easy, who would not know how to do it? [The other] said, "Indeed."
However, the Way is precisely where one must exert effort. Linquan said, "If you simply possess the heart of resolve, it will certainly not deceive you.

Yun said, "This [Way] cannot be pierced even by a needle; what effort could possibly be applied? Linquan said, "Though it is said to be without seams or gaps, how can one avoid being exposed and torn apart?
Yüan took his spade upon his shoulder and departed immediately. This may be called "not running while going downhill"—such a swift opportunity is difficult to encounter. —Taiyuan.

Venerable Fu could not restrain his indignation. He spoke on behalf [of the Master], saying: "The sacred remains of our former teacher still exist. In the forest and by the springs, one who sees injustice draws his sword to come to the aid.

Furthermore, he requested Danxia to re-proclaim this meaning, and offered this verse: The sacred remains of the former teacher still exist; In the forest and by the springs, one draws the sword to aid the cause. If you wish to know the meaning of the former teacher’s marrow, Look at the old woman selling radishes in the marketplace.

The fundamental ground is empty and luminous, without a single thing; (already too many have been born). How many people can recognize the golden bones? (It is not that they do not exist; it is simply that they are few.)
Carrying a spade upon his shoulder, he set off (treading with every step). Ta Bian was always as if mute (his true words were not acrid). The Master said:
"Formerly, when Minister Zhang had his residence burned down, he wrote a verse: 'The day the layman sank his boat, the minister lost his fire;
originally there was not a single thing—why use such bitter lamentation? The Sixth Patriarch also said: Bodhi..."
Originally there was no tree; the bright mirror is likewise not a stand. Originally there was not a single thing—how could one need to sweep away dust?
These lines all reveal the fundamental source-ground of the mind prior to the kalpa of emptiness. Were it not for possessing the adamantine eye, how could one recognize these golden bones?
Although this ground of ultimate reality does not admit even a speck of dust, why doubt its manifestation within the gate of Buddha-activity?
Without abandoning a single dharma—how much more so when holding a spade upon one’s shoulder? It is even more wondrous to turn back on the path, let go of the hand, and simply walk;
not dwelling in the position of correctness, great eloquence is like being mute. In silence, one knows for oneself that the field is secure. Great wisdom is like folly;

in a state of carefree ease, who would say the belly is stubborn? Do you know the point where letting go and gathering in are too swift? It is the same intent as when the spade was thrust in, and it is the same as when the spade is held.
The Mind. Look closely at this face-to-face presentation.
Case Seventeen: Dongshan’s "Early Autumn" (Untying the Knot).
He addressed the assembly, saying: "This side and that side—who can knock down the boundary wall? Going straight and coming from the side—try kicking it!"
Treading upon the fragrant grasses—how should one entrust this?

[The Master] cites Chan Master Dongshan Liangjie’s address to the assembly upon the conclusion of the summer retreat, saying: "At the beginning of autumn and the end of summer, you brothers may go east or west;
you must head toward a place ten thousand *li* away where there is not even an inch of grass. (A favorable condition is an unfavorable condition. After a long silence, he said:
"Just as it is in a place ten thousand *li* wide where there is not a single inch of grass—how does one proceed? (He awaits the instruction. Looking left and right, he said:
"If you wish to know this matter, you must be like flowers blooming upon a withered tree; only then will you accord with it" (when it is parched and dry, it must be moist;

in a place of cold stillness, warmth is required). Shishuang said: "Stepping out the door, there is grass" (to fall into the present moment is already permissible). Ming’an said: [He remained silent].
"Simply not going out the gate is also a sea of weeds (in the stillness of stagnant water, it is even more difficult to find sweetness).
The Master said, "The Great Perfect Enlightenment is my monastery. Why discuss east and west when the retreat is over?
Even if you were instructed to dwell in deep, hidden cold cliffs and gaze fully upon the cool greenery, sitting amidst white clouds will ultimately not be excellent. Guarding the cinnabar..."
It is lofty, yet not necessarily expedient. To teach people to point toward "silent stacking" (mo duo gen) is, in the end, a vain claim of antiquity.
Therefore, Dongshan feared they would fall into the realm of "nothingness," where cleverness turns into clumsiness and one forgets the way home like a lost child. After a long silence, he said:
"What about when there is not a single blade of grass for ten thousand miles—how do you proceed? This was all for the sake of raising his children; it was out of fear [of their falling into error].
To subdue the crafty is a matter of convenience; it is as the saying goes: "When a son travels a thousand *li*, his mother travels a thousand *li*.

Having reflected and reconsidered this again and again, he looked around left and right and said: "If you wish to know this matter, you must wait for flowers to bloom upon a withered tree before it will accord with the earth.
This can be called: "The correct, though correct, is yet biased; the biased, though biased, is yet round. One day, Yaoshan pointed to a withered tree and a flourishing tree.
Shanshan asked Daowu, "Which is it: the withered or the flourishing? Daowu said, "The flourishing.
Shanshan said, "Truly, in every place there is radiant brilliance. He then asked Yunyan, "Which is it: the withered or the flourishing? Yunyan said, "The withered.
Shanshan said, "Truly, in every place let it be left to wither away into stillness. Gao Sha... [text ends]
Mihu arrived suddenly. Baizhang asked, "Which is withered? Which is flourishing? Mihu replied, "As for the withered, let it be withered;
as for the flourishing, let it be flourishing. Baizhang turned back and said to Daowu and Yunyan, "Not so, not so.
In truth, this matter must be rolling and revolving, lively and agile—like a pearl rolling on a platter, leaving no trace of obstruction—only then is it acceptable. If one proceeds..."
He instructed him to go to a place where there is not even an inch of grass. How could a wedge driven into a rock ever be extracted?

To allow for the withered wood to sprout flowers is like granting the opening of a single thread. This led Shishuang to issue a reprimand, saying: "As soon as you step out the door, it is already grass.
If you merely give rise to a thought or stir a conception, is this not falling into the present moment? Later, Ming’an said: "It would have to be such that one does not even leave the door."
This is also a ground covered in thick grass. Although this is difficult to comprehend, it is actually the easiest to understand. Have you not heard it said:
"If one cuts down the cassia tree in the moon, its clear light will surely increase all the more"? Later, Tiantong provided a verse for both together: "Thick grass everywhere;

look for yourself at what is inside the gate and outside the gate. It is easy to set foot within a thicket of brambles, but difficult to turn one's body beyond the 'curtain of night-brightness. If..."
In discussing the single path of transforming the body, how could one avoid being pointed out by Danxia?

The verse says: How could one sit upon the emerald cloud-bed once home is reached? (Having been still for long, one longs for movement. How could one not walk upon the green grass when leaving the door? (Having been active for long, one longs for stillness. North, south, east, and west are fundamentally free;
(Having wandered for many days,) How can he, who has no front or back, be avoided? (The mind does not betray the person; the face shows no shame.)
The Master said: "Where not even a speck of dust is established, all things are silent and void. Having arrived here, the home is utterly emptied; thus one avoids being a fool within the house.
Though dwelling in the depths of the blue clouds, one must move the body with measured steps. When the bright moon shines, do not avoid entering the marketplace to extend a helping hand.
Since you have already departed from the land of Zhuzhu, why linger on the Hu-chuang? This is precisely 'not abiding in the correct.'"
This is a small model. Because the incoming breath does not dwell within the realms of the five aggregates, the outgoing breath does not involve itself with external conditions.
It is not that one loathes the "clamped bamboo and peach blossoms" upon the face; it is only for fear of the "heaven-piercing thorns" within the belly.
One never falls into the dull green gloom, nor is one willing to linger amidst the vast, lush verdure. Let there be desolate forests before one's eyes; let there be years of unrestrained wandering.
One might say: "Passing through a grove of a hundred flowers, not a single petal clings to one's body. This is the general outline of the principle of "not leaning toward the biased.
Those who have attained this are a thousandfold free and ten-thousandfold autonomous; they do not take root in stone chambers, but rather dwell for the night in grass huts.
Did you not see how Master Shitou was asked, "Will this hut fall apart or not? To which he replied, "It falls apart," and "It does not fall apart."
The indestructible Lord remains as he was; he dwells neither in the south, north, east, nor west. A firm foundation is what is most essential. It is also said:
"When light is turned back to reflect within, one returns home; the vast and penetrating spiritual root knows no turning away.
Looking at it this way, is there anything to avoid or not to avoid? Do you understand? When we meet, there is nothing to say; when we do not see him, we still ponder.
Case 18: Dongshan’s Great Matter (Attire).

Addressing the assembly, he said: "Look far, do not look near; in every thought, accord with the investigation of birth and death. Discuss the real, not the unreal; earnestly speak only of the ultimate truth.
Pointing it out clearly: buy later, taste first. For those who come to open their market stalls, here is the profit."
"Mm? Please, please proceed. [The Master] raised the case of Dongshan asking a monk:
"What thing in this world is most painful? (Do not let your emotions create obstructions; do not be deceived by your own tongue. The monk said, "Hell is the most painful.
(He knows only one, but does he know the other? Dongshan said, "Not so. You have not yet clarified it within this thread of the robe."
"A great matter begins with suffering (having once tasted it, one knows its sourness).
The Master said: "The Tathāgata delivers sentient beings by means of the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;
the Patriarchs develop the patch-robed monks by relying on the three untainted studies of precept, concentration, and wisdom. Dōngshān pointed his finger toward the summit of the highest mountain.
This monk has turned his head while at the bottom of the deep sea; he has already thanked him for it. He did not say that sugar is the sweetest or that Huangbo is the bitterest.
I suspect he cannot forget his familiar realm and even fears seeing the wardens of hell in his dreams.

Yet he does not know that Devadatta slandered the Buddha and fell into hell, where the Buddha ordered Ānanda to go to the prison and ask him, "Are you suffering? Devadatta replied: [The text provided ends here.]
"While I dwell within the Avīci Hell, it is as if I were experiencing the bliss of the Third Dhyāna Heaven; yet this monk says it is most painful.
Considering their respective capacities, how vast is the difference between them, like that between heaven and earth! Thus Dongshan said: "It is not so.

It is only when one does not clarify the Great Matter beneath these robes that it is truly suffering. This is truly what is meant by: "Out of pity for a three-year-old child, one exhausts the heart of a lifetime."
Although this is like an ox eating grass at its own head, what harm is there in adding spots to a tiger’s back? Fortunately, we encountered Danxia, who offered mutual admonition.
The verse says: “How many kinds of boiling cauldrons and burning coals are there?
(To see them, the eyes dazzle; to contemplate them, the mind is disturbed. The three miserable realms and the hells are not yet so bitter and sour. (This offends the ear...)
These are words of loyalty. You must believe the intimate words from Xinfeng (and keep them clearly in mind). Do not be negligent beneath the *kāṣāya* (do not allow yourself to forget).
The Master said: "The entire ocean of karmic obstructions arises solely from deluded thoughts.

How could it be limited merely to the bitter sufferings of the hells, the three evil paths, the cauldrons of boiling water, the furnaces of burning coals, the sword-trees, and the blade-mountains? For this reason, Danxia took the place of Dongshan to restate this meaning, speaking once more in verse:
'The ancients and those of later generations shared a most earnest, grandmotherly heart; for the most part, they were concerned with the cycle of rebirth within the six realms.'"
Appearing and disappearing within the four modes of birth, all are due to their failure to understand the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye and the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*.
When the World-Honored One first attained perfect enlightenment, he universally observed that all sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of a Tathāgata;
yet, because of deluded thoughts and attachments, they do not realize it. Is this not what Dongshan referred to as the "Great Matter"? Therefore, once again...
The Third Entrustment: One must believe the intimate words of Xinfeng; do not be negligent beneath the *kāṣāya*.
During the late Dazhong era of the Tang dynasty, Dongshan received and guided students at Mount Xinfeng. Subsequently, his teachings flourished at Dongshan in Gao’an, Yuzhang.

There, he provisionally established the five ranks (*wùwèi*), skillfully accommodated the three capacities (*sāngēn*), extensively propagated the profound resonance, and gloriously upheld the ancestral Way.
Therefore, the mountain where he resided came to be known by the name Xinfeng (New Abundance).

As for the words of his final instruction—whether they were intimate or not, whether they were to be taken as broad and general or not—it is like a person drinking water: what need is there to ask about its warmth or cold?
Only the mind itself knows. *Vūtangjí*, Scroll One.

The Bodhisattva then relinquished his celestial lifespan. That night, the Holy Queen dreamed that the Bodhisattva, riding upon a sandalwood pavilion atop a sun-disk king-elephant, entered her right flank.
When the time arrived, she went to the Lumbinī Garden beneath an *aśoka* tree;

its flowers were in full bloom, and as the Queen reached out her hand to pluck one, the Holy One manifested birth from her right flank. This was during the twenty-fourth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty.
On the eighth day of the fourth month of that year, divine dragons sent down water to bathe him; the earth surged forth golden lotuses to support him.
He walked seven paces in every direction, pointing with his fingers to heaven and earth, and let out a lion’s roar: "In all the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am honored."

Later, he left the household life, scaled the city walls, and went to Mount Daṇḍaka to practice the path. First, he stayed with Ārāḍa Kālāma for three years, where he studied the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*);

realizing it was not the ultimate truth, he abandoned it. He then went to Udraka Rāmaputra for three years, where he studied the meditative attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*);

realizing this too was not the goal, he abandoned it as well. Subsequently, he went to Mount Gajaśīrṣa and, together with various non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*), subsisted on a daily diet of hemp and wheat.
This lasted for six years. Thus, a sutra says: "By means of being without mind or intention and without the practice of reception, he completely subdued all non-Buddhists.

Having first undergone trials of heterodox methods, he demonstrated various skillful means and aroused diverse views, leading them to Bodhi. The *Pujipin Jing* (Sutra on the Universal Collection) states:
"On the eighth day of the second month, at the time when the morning star appeared, the Bodhisattva attained the Unsurpassed Way and was titled 'Heavenly and Human [Teacher].'"
The Master was then thirty years of age. It was the second year of King Mu’s reign, the year of *Guiwei*.
Subsequently, within the Deer Park, he turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths for the five disciples, including Kauṇḍinya, and they all realized the fruits of the Path.
From Magadha to Vārāṇasī, and finally reaching Kuśinagara, his work of transforming sentient beings was completed. He manifested the appearance of illness at the [Hiraṇyavatī] River.
Between the twin *śāla* trees by the riverbank, he lay on his right side with his feet stacked, profoundly and serenely in great stillness (*mahāśānti*).
All of these were means of manifesting signs to entice the deluded and guide sentient beings. To deliberate upon them or to recognize and cling to them is to miss the mark entirely.
It is said: "The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata. One must realize that this cuts off the path of language; it is neither coming nor going.
Now, dwelling thus: "In this hall, the wind is cold and faint; through the ages, the meaning remains clear.
The Eighty-fourth Case: Guangde’s Long-Term Burden (The Mirror-Fan).
He addressed the assembly, saying: "A priceless jewel is buried within one's clothing, yet one willingly endures poverty—how pitiable is such delusion!"
One morning, when the wine has worn off, one finally believes that those who know one’s heart do not turn their backs. Is there anyone here with the true eye?

A monk asked Guangde, “When one has long been burdened by the failure to meet [the right person] at the right time, what then? (This is enough to make one feel abashed. Guangde said, “The fan is opened, yet people do not encounter it;
in the humble alley, no one can gather it up. (Difficult to find the perfect fit.)
The Master said: "The luminous pearl of the mind pierces the Dipper and Ox; its secret depths have remained hidden for many autumns.

Alas, those mired in worldly delusion find it hard to recognize; though presented face-to-face, they simply let it pass. This is because their sentiments harbor preferences and aversions, and their views and attachments are biased and parched."
Although one may have long intended to do so, how can one avoid missing the mark right at the head?

If you understand how to guard the beginning and protect the end, returning to the root and restoring the source, you will recognize the old monk at the tip of every blade of grass and identify the Son of Heaven in the midst of a bustling marketplace. Have you not seen what the Bagua (Pudai) Upadhyaya said:
"Maitreya is truly Maitreya; he manifests a thousand million transformations. From time to time he shows himself to those of this age, yet those of this age..."

None recognized him. They vied with one another to avoid Emperor Wu’s path, saying, "To see him is not to see him; to meet him is not to meet him. Whether in the present or the past, they only regretted and lamented it.
When this monk asked his question, he was judging others by his own standard. Since he had already surrendered his head, how could it concern my affairs?
Thus, the Way of Broad Virtue is fanned open for people; had they not encountered it in the humble alley, it could not have been gathered.
This too is a case of being situated in a partial place yet not missing the fundamental intent within the Mysterious. Though hidden, it is ever more manifest; though revealed, it is never exposed.
One must also possess the fixed, singular eye of the school to perceive it. The verse says:

The wondrous body is majestic and grand, with all the marks and signs complete (it cannot be depicted nor painted). Walking alone across the azure sky, he treads upon golden lotuses (Siddhārtha still remains).

One is still loath to sit upon the thousand-petaled lotus pedestal (for one has already shed the mundane and left the secular); how could one be willing to wear a tattered, soiled robe (as the Sūtra says:
"it does not stick to skin or cling to bone")?
The Master said: "Stately and magnificent, towering and dignified—possessing the marks of a great man, with ten thousand virtues fully manifest.

This is not something acquired in a morning or an evening; it is the mark of the wondrous essence long nurtured within. Indeed, from time immemorial, this has been inherently present in every person and lacking in none.
It is only that people fail to honor their own spiritual nature and bury their family treasure. When will they ever [realize this]?"
Walking alone across the azure heavens, his feet tread upon golden lotuses. Thus it is said: "So lofty that it cannot be pointed out; so profound that it is difficult to fathom.
Upon the terrace of a thousand flowers, he is too weary to sit upon the bed of both the Correct and the Deviant; before the steps of a hundred jewels, he is too tired to walk upon the fragrant grass.
How much more so when one emerges in tattered, stained robes with sagging collars and sleeves—acting improperly and bringing disgrace upon the family tradition. How pitiable! To remain...
Amidst the dust of sensual passion, one suffers and rushes about within the confines of form and shadow.

Though this is nothing but bumping one's head and striking one's forehead, it is still like a son turning his back on his father to seek out his stepmother. If you analyze the groves and springs in this manner, do you recognize them or not?
Where each and every thing is revealed, observe closely and thoroughly.
Case Eighty-Five: Waves of Vast Virtue (The Boat and Oars).
Guangde addressed the assembly, saying: "Vast and expansive, boundless and surging; shoreless and limitless, neither shallow nor deep.
Is there anyone who can cross over by cutting through the current?"
A monk asked Chan Master Guangde Zhou: "How can one attain the wondrous within the midst of waves? (The wind-power supports the sail so it travels without oars;
the sound of the flute calls one down to Cangzhou under the moon. Guangde said: "Oars and paddles are not employed, and the bottom is cast off; coming and going, one never relies on a life-raft.
(Though it is said one must use a raft to cross the river, who knows that once the shore is reached, the boat is no longer needed?)
The Master said: "The source of the mind is vast and boundless; the ocean of nature is clear and still.

Yet, when consciousness and intellect are stirred up, the winds of karma blow and drift, causing the six realms and four modes of birth to sink and wallow in birth and death with no prospect of escape. As the ancients did not say:

'Setting sail upon the ship of ignorance, one follows the current of nescience into the sea of birth and death'? This monk’s inquiry likely stems from being afflicted by this malady, and thus he seeks the wondrous medicine."

"Using vast virtue to cultivate and synthesize according to the directions, one evaluates the Path through direct realization. Without employing oars or paddles, and with both bottom and sides detached, one never relies on a life-preserving float in coming and going.
As for Guangde’s speaking thus—does he answer his interlocutor’s words?
Does he speak for him? Is this talk beyond the ordinary? Or is it a deliberation upon the immediate? Let those with eyes discern and examine it; they do not see Dongshan.
The Way: Be most careful not to seek it from another; to do so would distance you from me. Now I go forth alone, and everywhere I encounter Him.
He is now truly myself, yet I am not now He. You must understand it in this way before you can realize Suchness.
At that time, Dongshan passed through water and saw his reflection, attaining great enlightenment. Is this not finding the wondrous within the waves?
This is so. Since Dongshan possessed such supernatural powers and attained the Great Samādhi, why would he need to rely on a life-preserving float to cross over?
As for all other matters where the Way has not yet reached, he entrusted them to Danxia. The verse says:
A single phrase in response is difficult to grasp (yet one must avoid speaking of it). The Wheel-Turning King does not transform the land of Jambudvīpa (for supreme governance is non-action).

Boundless lands are as level as the ripples on the ocean waves (viewing them as a single body). Riding alone a clay ox to plow the moonlight (only when there is no strength is there true achievement).
The Master said: "The three phrases clarify the one phrase; the one phrase clarifies the three phrases. One and three do not interfere with one another—this is clearly the path that transcends.
But as for this path that transcends, what is it like? To ascend and step out the door, it is all the road to Chang’an.
Fasten your straw sandals securely and walk slowly. Is such a response worthy of being taken as a standard, or is it not?"

Let everyone try to settle this and observe it for themselves. If you can indeed settle it, then it will be like the appearance of a Wheel-Turning King in the world who brings about transformation through non-action;
throughout Jambudvīpa, there is no governance yet no disorder. There is trust without words, and practice without instruction.
Even if the boundless oceans of lands were not all wind-stilled and wave-quieted, though one may alone drive the clay ox to plow the moonlight,
letting it freely emerge from nothingness and grasp the clouds within emptiness— never violating the musical scales, one sings and plays by oneself.
One might say that the words carry the profound mystery yet leave no path; the tongue speaks, yet there is nothing spoken.

At such a time, one must forget all achievements and transcend both speech and silence, emerging from right and wrong and departing from gain and loss. Apply your full attention to investigate and examine this, and you will see the needlework of Danxia.
Do you understand it clearly? "Needling twin phoenixes with eyesightless—soaring into the void, piercing the azure heavens."

Village Li Er-lang). The Master said:

The fundamental Buddha-nature of all sentient beings is likewise so. At that time, Master Fenyang Shao, while among the assembly, stepped forward and asked: "The bright moon..."

beyond the realm of Jambudvīpa, one ascends freely. [The questioner] said: "A bottomless bowl transmitted by the thousand sages—everyone of this age sings the Song of Great Peace.
He asked: "How does one sing the tune of Great Peace? He replied: "It does not fall into the five musical notes; it has nothing to do with them."
Sixth, regarding the *lǜ* (musical scales/monastic regulations): "Is there anyone who can attain harmony with them? He replied, "I pray that the Master will not withhold his compassion.

Master Zhigong called out, "Yun Guang! The ox raised its head. The Master said, "Why do you not speak? You pull, yet it is not pulling.

The corners are distinct; I grant him this. Therefore, Shimen said: "In a humble alley, one does not ride a golden horse;

Entering the marketplace with hands extended, the compassionate heart is profound. Do not harbor false suspicions when facing such an occasion. Fortunately, there was Danxia.
On behalf of this snow-buck, I offer this verse:
Amidst the groves of auspicious grass, he is too weary to sleep (let him leap as he pleases). Strolling leisurely wherever he may, he moves with effortless ease (transcending all constraints).
Clad in fur and bearing horns, he is difficult for men to recognize (rare indeed is the clear mirror). I tell you, young boy, there is no need for the whip (why exhaust your strength?).
The Master said: "This dull-witted, ignorant water buffalo—how could it ever consent to mingle with the common herd? Why labor to pasture it here and there by the stream?
Once the nose-rope is loosened, the six senses cannot be restrained. Thus, amidst the cluster of auspicious grasses, it is too weary to sleep, yet wanders with ease and autonomy;
within the rows of sacred sprouts, it takes a step or two, roaming at will and free from care. It comes here with deliberate intent."

Walking slowly toward it, everyone felt a sense of carefree liberation; there was nothing but a state of vast openness and tranquil ease. With clouds over the ridges and the moon over the fields, they were transcendent in their lack of effortful achievement;
though wearing horns and shrouded in fur, they subtly penetrated the profound mysteries. The calligraphy of Master Miu contained the meaning within its strokes;
the old man Wang’s horizontal posture revealed that the truth lay inside. Why seek it by having a child with a whip urge it forth? There is no need for a wild father to do so.
Grieving over the weeding: the ground of the empty kalpa has neither boundary nor limit; the tree at its center is neither flourishing nor withered.

Let them tread upon it as they will, yet watch me pull it forth. It does not fall into the present moment while remaining in the present, nor does it dwell outside of phenomena while remaining outside of phenomena.
It is not merely a matter of being leisurely and at ease; it is, rather, a state of exhilaration and joy. Just as it is so, do you understand how to make use of it?
When hungry, eat the tender grass without restraint; when thirsty, drink the cold spring water, coming and going as you please.
Case Eighty-Seven: The Family of Count Taiyuan (The Offering of Porridge).

Venerable Lu went daily to receive offerings from households across the four continents; how could it have been limited to just a few families? This monk has a small vessel and lacks great capacity;

Were it not for Taoyuan, it would have been difficult to respond to this. Although it is said that "the moon reflects in the waters of a thousand rivers, and every door has its monk," this was long ago.

If you can transcend the realm of conceptualization and leave behind verbal explanations, suddenly grasping the pattern beyond the boundaries of speech and silence, then you will not be like one who breaks a pearl to seek its reflection or marks a boat with a tally while searching for a lost sword.
For the time being, turn toward the path of the present moment to call out "one" and shout "six," matching the purple and drawing the lot.
Qing: Do not immediately offer some ready-made, conventional talk that is like a tethering stake for a donkey—just collapsing everything.

When Old Man Shun first came from Dongshan to Wuchang to beg for alms, he went first to the home of a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*). This layman was a man of high conduct, respected by the entire prefecture;

Not knowing his full realization, the master treated him with some degree of ease. The layman said, "I, an old man, have a phrase to ask of you, Venerable Sir.
If our words accord, I shall open my robe; if they do not accord, I ask that you return it to Xinfeng. He asked, "When an ancient mirror has already been polished, how is it?
[The master] replied, "It illuminates heaven and earth. He asked, "Before it was polished, how was it? [The master] replied, "Black as lacquer. The layman said, "But..."
"Please return to the mountain. Shun immediately hurried back and recounted the incident to Chan Master Cong. Cong spoke on his behalf.

Shun then went to question him, saying, "What is it like when the ancient mirror has not yet been polished? Cong said, "It is not far from here to Hanyang. [Shun asked again,] "What is it like after it has been polished?"

Wondrously perfect and formless, he existed before the kalpas; (meeting face-to-face yet not seeing each other). According to types, he expediently divided himself into ten billion forms;
(constantly appearing to people of the age, yet no one recognized him). At moonlit night, as the tower announces the break of dawn, (he secretly penetrates the workings of transformation);

The Master said: Chan Master Weize of Fuku Yan on Mount Tiantai stated, "Heaven and earth are without things; things and the self are without things.
Although they are without things, they have never been without things. If this is so, then the sage is like a shadow and the common people are like a dream—who could undergo birth and death?
Furthermore, in the wondrous, perfect, and formless state prior to the kalpa of emptiness, there was no person."

The Great can be manifested; it is not something that can be constructed or assembled from the six sense faculties. It is without shadow, without form, without demonstration, and without consciousness.
Although it is said that the Sage has no self, how could one know that there is nowhere he does not manifest himself?

Thus, he is able to provisionally divide his body into a thousand, ten thousand, or a hundred million forms according to the various types [of beings], such that every atom and every world is so. At this moment, though we have briefly parted from the kalpa of emptiness, how could there be any interval in his reaching down his hand to save humanity?

It is as clear as the moonlit night when the dripping water-clock sounds stretch for a mere foot or two; the tower announces dawn, and at first light, spring meets us everywhere across the six realms.
Only then can one believe that the One Qi speaks not, yet contains all forms; where could the myriad spirits go to thank its impartiality?
Case Eighty-Eight: Liangshan’s Daily Use (Addressing the Occasion).
He addressed the assembly, saying: "Opening the mouth to eat, not a single grain of rice is ever chewed; extending the hand to dress, not a single thread of silk is ever hung upon.
Do you understand this state where one attains the wondrous in every movement and encounters the source on every side?"
A monk asked Chan Master Liangshan Guan, "What is the matter of daily life? (Every point constantly manifests; every thing is entirely pervasive.
Shan said, "Jade-green points pierce through the color of lapis lazuli; before one's eyes, amidst the red dust, not a grain of sand is seen. (The pointing-out is clear and distinct.)

"What do you mean by 'mutual entry'? The seated assembly looked at one another in great astonishment and none could offer an answer. Zhen said, "The joy of the road does not mean one has reached home;
insight that merely penetrates the subtle is not called seeing the Way. One must investigate with true investigation; one must awaken with true awakening."
"King Yama does not fear much talk. Linquan said: "Bitter words are good medicine; harsh speech is loyal counsel.
Only when one truly realizes the principle of consciousness-only and mind-only will there be nothing within the square inch of the heart that can cause obstruction.
Thus Baoshou said: 'Clouds arise beyond the railing; raindrops fall from the eaves. The mountain stream is as clear as indigo; the wild [flowers]..."
The blossoms bloom as if woven. Master Shou’s *Secret Instruction on the Mind-Only* also says: "The trees upon the crags and the branches in the courtyard each manifest boundless wondrous forms;
the cries of monkeys and the songs of birds all discourse upon the perfect sound of non-duality. Is this not indeed the case that every speck of dust is thus, and every dharma is thus?
If you should miss the mark here, it would be a waste to wait for the Dragon Flower Assembly; it is better to return to your respective quarters to avoid [this error].
Having stood for a long time, Baoshou was thus filled with compassion; how could Danxia not offer praise? He spoke in verse:

"Vividly transcending past, present, and future—(where a single word cuts off the path, the meaning of a thousand ages is clear). The entire triple world is but a single point of mind—(if you recognize it, it is still not it).
Outside the railing, peach blossoms and spring butterflies dance—(when form is form, speak lightly of understanding). Before the gate, willow trees..."
The Dawn Cuckoo’s Song (Examine closely where sound is not sound). The Master said:
"The nature of awakening is perfectly luminous and its spiritual knowing is never obscured. Throughout the ten ages of past and present, there is nothing that is not fully complete.

In the past of the past, it is like a thunderclap striking the true void; in the future of the future, it is like waves subsiding into the water of nature. How could this apply only to the realm of desire?"
The realms of form and formlessness are subsumed within a single mind; even the entirety of the dharma-realm of space is encompassed by the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of consciousness-only.
Yet, how could one know this? When a monk asked Master Jiao of Langya, "If it is fundamentally pure and serene, why do mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
Jiao replied, "If it is fundamentally pure and serene, why do mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? This is what [the text] refers to.
It is said that when deluded, the three realms exist; once awakened, the ten directions are empty.

As for the peach blossoms outside the railing and the willows before the gate, let the butterflies dance at their leisure and the orioles sing their fill—what need is there to concern oneself with them?
To hear without hearing and to listen without listening, where sound and form are pure and true, leaving no room for divergent thoughts. Can you still do so? Mountains, rivers, and grasses...
The True Principle is Exalted by Wood; the Flower-Moon Pavilion Proclaims the Sublime Sound.
Recorded Commentary on Chan Master Danxia Chun’s *Virtuous Hall Collection* of Verses on Ancient Cases, Volume Six (End). By the Elder of Forest and Spring.
